stories.headline: Colombian Presidential Election Marred by Ecuador Interference Accusations Ahead of Sunday Vote
stories.summary:
Colombia's foreign ministry has accused Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa of deliberate interference in its presidential election, scheduled for Sunday, after Noboa publicly promised right-wing Colombian candidate Abelardo de la Espriella he would lift tariffs on Colombian goods as of June 1 — framing the conversation as one with an "administration-in-waiting." Colombia's government called the move "a flagrant violation of the principle of non-intervention" and "an attack on the democratic system."

Colombia is headed into a deeply polarized election following the presidency of left-wing Gustavo Petro, who is constitutionally barred from seeking re-election. Polling suggests Petro's chosen successor, Iván Cepeda, leads the field, with de la Espriella as his closest rival. No candidate is expected to win an outright majority, making a June 21 runoff highly likely. The election's outcome could significantly reshape Colombia's foreign alignments, particularly its relationships with the United States and regional neighbors.

Noboa, a close U.S. ally who has taken a hardline stance on drug cartel violence, has joined a U.S.-led regional anti-cartel alliance. His intervention reflects the broader geopolitical contest playing out across Latin America between left-leaning governments aligned with Petro's model and right-leaning administrations aligned with Washington. The tariff dispute stems from Ecuador's long-running accusations that Colombia has failed to secure their shared border, which serves as a corridor for cocaine trafficking.

stories.headline: PSG Wins Back-to-Back UEFA Champions League Titles With Penalty Shootout Victory Over Arsenal
stories.summary:
Paris Saint-Germain claimed back-to-back UEFA Champions League titles on Saturday, defeating Arsenal 4-3 on penalties in Budapest following a 1-1 draw after extra time. The result marks a historic moment for the French club, which has invested heavily in transforming itself into a European powerhouse following years of near-misses in the competition's latter stages.

The win consolidates PSG's standing as one of European football's dominant forces and delivers a second consecutive continental crown — a rare achievement in the modern era of the Champions League. Arsenal, seeking their first-ever Champions League title, were denied in dramatic fashion. The match drew a massive global television audience and stands as one of the most significant results in either club's recent history.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. Military Drug-Boat Strikes Push Death Toll Past 200 in Monthslong Campaign
stories.summary:
The U.S. military carried out another strike Friday on an alleged drug-smuggling vessel in the eastern Pacific Ocean, killing three men and pushing the overall death toll from the monthslong campaign to 202 people. U.S. Southern Command announced the strike, saying the vessel was operated by a designated terrorist organization and engaged in narco-trafficking operations, though it provided no independent evidence. The latest attack was notable for being the first released in color video footage rather than the usual black-and-white imagery.

The strikes, which began in early September, have accelerated this week, with three separate attacks announced Tuesday, Wednesday, and Friday. The Trump administration has declared the United States to be in an armed conflict with Latin American drug cartels, arguing they are responsible for the flow of narcotics into American communities. Critics have raised due process concerns, noting the military provides no judicial finding before lethal strikes on civilian vessels at sea.

The announcement came as Gen. Francis L. Donovan, the top U.S. commander in Latin America, met with Cuban military leaders near the U.S. Navy base at Guantanamo Bay on Friday — a notable diplomatic contact given the historically strained U.S.-Cuba relationship. The campaign has drawn comparatively little congressional debate despite its scale, with more than 200 people killed by U.S. military action outside of any formally declared war zone.

stories.headline: Trump Receives Clean Bill of Health After Walter Reed Physical; Cognitive Test Administered
stories.summary:
White House physician Dr. Sean Barbabella declared President Donald Trump in "excellent health" and "fully fit to carry out all duties of the Commander-in-Chief" following a physical examination at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center — Trump's third in-person medical checkup in 13 months and his fourth hospital visit of his second term. The assessment, released Friday, noted the president underwent a cognitive test as part of the evaluation.

The memo acknowledged some physical findings, including lower leg swelling and bruising on his hand, though the physician characterized these as non-disqualifying. The release of a presidential health assessment carries particular political weight following bipartisan criticism over what many lawmakers described as the concealment of President Biden's declining health during his term — criticism that intensified after Jill Biden's recent public admission that she feared her husband was having a stroke during the 2024 presidential debate.

Presidential health disclosures have become a heightened point of public and congressional interest, with both parties facing questions about transparency regarding the fitness of aging leaders. Trump, who turned 79 this month, has consistently disputed characterizations of health concerns, and the White House released the physician's memo publicly rather than waiting for press inquiries.

stories.headline: AUKUS Partners Announce Underwater Drone Program to Protect Undersea Cables and Counter Maritime Threats
stories.summary:
The United States, United Kingdom, and Australia announced Saturday at the Shangri-La Dialogue security summit in Singapore that they will jointly develop uncrewed undersea vehicle technology under their AUKUS military alliance, with the systems expected to be operational by next year. The program represents the first signature deliverable under AUKUS Pillar Two, which focuses on advanced capabilities beyond the pact's flagship nuclear submarine initiative. The UK will contribute £150 million ($201 million) to the effort.

The underwater drones are designed to protect seabed infrastructure such as undersea cables and pipelines, conduct surveillance and reconnaissance, and carry out strike operations. UK Defence Secretary John Healey acknowledged prior criticism of AUKUS's pace, saying "for too long in Aukus, we talked too much and delivered too little," adding that the situation had changed. The announcement follows Healey's accusation in April that Russia was running a covert operation targeting cables and pipelines north of the UK — an allegation Moscow has denied.

The program is widely interpreted as a counter to both Russian and Chinese undersea activities, though the three defence ministers declined to confirm this framing when questioned by reporters. China is suspected of damaging cables near Taiwan and in Swedish waters, while multiple Baltic Sea cable incidents have also been reported. The technology will be deployed across the Pacific, Atlantic, and High North waters.

stories.headline: Artists Withdraw From Trump-Linked Freedom 250 Celebration; President Threatens to Convert Event Into Rally
stories.summary:
Multiple performers booked for Freedom 250's Great American State Fair — a 16-day event planned on the National Mall in Washington between June 25 and July 10 celebrating the nation's 250th birthday — have pulled out, saying they were misled about the event's political affiliation. Artists including the Commodores, Poison frontman Bret Michaels, country singer Martina McBride, Young MC, and Morris Day announced their withdrawals, with several stating they agreed to perform at what they believed was a nonpartisan event.

Freedom 250 was launched last year by the Trump administration, and the president appointed its CEO, though the organization describes itself as a nonprofit "dedicated to uniting Americans around the nation's 250th anniversary." President Trump responded Saturday on Truth Social, calling the departing performers "third rate" and saying he was considering converting the occasion into an "America Is Back Rally" at the same time and location, declaring himself the "Number One Attraction anywhere in the World."

Some performers are standing by their commitments. Vanilla Ice, still slated to perform, said "This is not a political platform. This is celebrating America's birthday." Flo Rida also remains on the lineup. The episode highlights the tension surrounding the administration's use of the sesquicentennial anniversary celebrations, with critics arguing the event blurs the line between national commemoration and partisan politics, while supporters contend opponents are politicizing a patriotic celebration.

stories.headline: Ghana Parliament Passes Bill Criminalizing Homosexuality With Up to Three Years in Prison
stories.summary:
Ghana's parliament on Saturday approved legislation criminalizing homosexuality and the promotion of LGBTQ+ activities, with penalties of up to three years in prison for anyone who identifies as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, or queer. The bill also introduces a "duty to report" prohibited acts to police and would make supporting LGBTQ+ individuals as an "ally" a criminal offense, with limited exemptions for legal, medical, and media professionals.

The legislation now awaits ratification by President John Dramani Mahama, who has signaled his support, stating after taking office that he believes "only two genders exist" and that marriage is between a man and a woman. Religious leaders have been a driving force behind the bill's passage, arguing it protects Ghanaian family and cultural values.

International human rights organizations, including Human Rights Watch, sharply criticized the measure, warning it places LGBTQ+ people's lives at risk and "encourages citizens to surveil and denounce one another." The organization formally recommended the bill be abandoned during committee review.

Ghana passed a similar bill in 2024, but it lapsed when the previous president did not sign it amid legal challenges. The new law is part of a broader trend across parts of Africa, with Senegal passing comparable legislation in March and Uganda introducing the death penalty for certain same-sex acts in 2023.

stories.headline: Philippines Seeks Closer Military Ties With Taiwan and China's Adversaries; China Expels NYT Journalist Over Taiwan Interview
stories.summary:
The Philippines is actively pursuing closer defense ties with Taiwan and stronger military links with nations focused on countering China's "nefarious plans," according to the Southeast Asian nation's defense chief. The move signals a deepening strategic alignment between Manila and parties at odds with Beijing amid continued tensions in the South China Sea.

In a related development, China expelled a New York Times journalist from the country after the newspaper published an interview with Taiwan's president, in what Beijing described as part of its campaign to isolate the self-governed island on the world stage. The expulsion marks a significant escalation in China's use of media access as a diplomatic pressure tool.

The developments come against the backdrop of Secretary Hegseth's participation in the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore this week, where U.S. and regional officials have been navigating a shifting American posture toward China following the Trump-Xi summit in Beijing. The Philippines, a U.S. treaty ally, has been a focal point of Indo-Pacific tension as Chinese vessels have repeatedly clashed with Filipino coast guard ships near disputed shoals.

Taiwan's government has not publicly commented on the Philippines outreach, but the moves collectively illustrate the degree to which smaller Indo-Pacific nations are recalibrating their security postures as great-power competition intensifies in the region.

stories.headline: Update: Former CDC Director Warns Congo Ebola Outbreak Could Become Second Largest in History
stories.summary:
Former CDC Director Robert Redfield issued a stark warning Friday that the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo could surpass all but one outbreak in recorded history. Redfield told NewsNation the outbreak is already the third-largest ever recorded, with WHO figures showing suspected cases surpassing 1,000 and nearly 250 suspected deaths. The outbreak is growing rapidly despite international attention.

The warning comes as the Trump administration has drawn criticism from infectious disease experts for what they describe as an increasingly isolationist response to the crisis. Countries around the world have mobilized funds and personnel, but experts say the global response is being outpaced by the spread of the disease.

The Ebola situation has already prompted a series of domestic policy responses, including enhanced screening at JFK and other airports for travelers from affected nations, and a previously reported — and subsequently blocked — plan to establish a quarantine facility in Kenya for exposed Americans. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus traveled to Bunia in the DRC, the epicenter of the outbreak, underscoring the severity of the situation.

Public health officials have expressed concern that without a more aggressive international response, including access to vaccines and medicines that remain in short supply, the outbreak's trajectory could worsen significantly in the coming weeks.

stories.headline: Nvidia Set to Debut First Windows PCs Powered by Its Chips Next Week
stories.summary:
Nvidia is expected to unveil the first Windows computers running its chips as the primary processor at two major industry conferences next week, Axios reported Friday, citing sources familiar with the plans. Microsoft will jointly present the initiative, marking a significant expansion of Nvidia's reach beyond its dominant position in AI data center hardware into the consumer and enterprise PC market.

The move gives Microsoft a second opportunity to establish itself in the AI PC segment after its initial push stumbled. Nvidia's involvement lends the effort substantial credibility given the company's standing as the world's most valuable chipmaker and the central supplier of hardware powering the AI boom.

The announcement is expected to intensify competition in the PC processor market, where Qualcomm has been pushing its Arm-based chips for AI-capable Windows laptops. Intel and AMD, the traditional dominators of the Windows PC chip space, could face new pressure if Nvidia's entry gains commercial traction.

Details on which PC manufacturers will launch devices using the new Nvidia chips — and at what price points — were not disclosed ahead of the formal announcement, but Dell is among the partners expected to be involved, according to Axios.

stories.headline: ICE Eyes Selling Mega-Warehouses Bought Under Noem for Mass Detention
stories.summary:
The Trump administration is considering selling several of the large warehouses that Immigration and Customs Enforcement purchased earlier this year under former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, according to two DHS officials cited by NBC News. The facilities were intended to serve as mega-detention centers capable of holding up to 8,000 immigrants each, part of a broader plan to reach a total detention capacity of 100,000 people nationwide. The total cost of the warehouse acquisitions was estimated at over $38 billion.

DHS officials said ICE no longer believes it needs that level of capacity, a statement that reflects a cultural shift inside the department since Secretary Markwayne Mullin took over from Noem. The potential sale of assets also follows President Trump's comment that he may want a "softer touch" on immigration enforcement, a remark that came after two U.S. citizens were fatally shot during immigration enforcement operations in Minneapolis in January.

The administration is also reportedly considering selling planes purchased or leased under Noem's leadership, including a luxury Boeing 737 Max 8. ICE has historically relied on chartered aircraft for deportations, and the planes acquired during Noem's tenure were the first to be government-owned.

The warehouses had been highly controversial at the local level, drawing protests and dividing communities over economic and humanitarian concerns. Even some Republicans opposed facilities planned for their districts, and Maryland successfully sued to block development of a warehouse near Hagerstown. A DHS spokesperson said the department is "assessing all resources" to "maximize efficiency" under new leadership.

stories.headline: Ukraine Deploying AI-Enabled Drones to Systematically Strike Russian Supply Convoys
stories.summary:
Ukraine's military has significantly escalated a campaign to destroy Russian logistics convoys in occupied territory using new AI-enabled drone technology, with BBC Verify confirming footage of at least 14 vehicle strikes along critical supply routes in the past week alone. The targeted routes connect Russia to Crimea and other occupied southern Ukrainian territories and are essential for feeding, fueling, and arming Russian front-line units. Analysts say the strikes are part of a deliberate "logistics lockdown" strategy announced by Ukraine's defense minister.

The AI-enabled Hornet drone system allows Ukraine to strike Russian targets at greater distances and with increased accuracy than previously possible. Conflict analysts have confirmed destruction of at least 150 vehicles more than 20 kilometers from the front line, though experts believe this represents roughly half of all actual incidents. Russia has reportedly responded by shortening convoy lengths to reduce exposure.

The campaign comes as analysis from the Institute for the Study of War indicates Ukraine is beginning to retake more ground than it is losing for the first time since 2023. Land warfare experts note that cutting resupply lines — including ammunition trucks operating 100 kilometers or more from the front — represents a qualitatively new capability that could degrade Russia's ability to sustain offensive operations.

Ukraine's defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, framed the drone strikes as intended to "deny the enemy the ability to conduct sustained offensive operations." The development adds a significant new dimension to the conflict at a moment when diplomatic efforts, including ceasefire discussions, remain unresolved.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. and Iran Reach Tentative 60-Day Ceasefire Extension, Hormuz Reopening Terms Set
stories.summary:
U.S. and Iranian negotiators reached a tentative agreement Thursday to extend the 3-month-old ceasefire by 60 days and launch a new round of talks on Iran's nuclear program, according to a U.S. official familiar with the matter. Vice President JD Vance confirmed the tentative deal but said it remained unclear whether President Trump would approve it, noting that negotiators were still working through disputed language points.

Under the emerging memorandum of understanding, Iran would be prohibited from imposing tolls on the Strait of Hormuz and required to remove all mines from the critical waterway within 30 days. In return, the U.S. would gradually lift its naval blockade on Iranian ports and relax sanctions, allowing Iran to sell more oil. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent predicted oil prices could 'come down very quickly' once a final deal is in place.

Iran had not publicly confirmed the deal as of Friday. The ceasefire has been under strain, with Kuwait intercepting Iranian missiles less than 24 hours before the agreement was announced. Iran has been allowing roughly two dozen commercial vessels daily through the Strait — compared with more than 100 before the war — and had established a formal gatekeeper agency to charge tolls, prompting a fresh round of U.S. sanctions this week.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of the world's traded oil and natural gas flows, has been effectively closed since the war began in late February, driving energy prices sharply higher globally. A finalized deal would represent a significant diplomatic development, though both sides have previously traded accusations of bad faith, and the agreement still requires approval from both Trump and Iran's leadership.

stories.headline: Louisiana Passes New Congressional Map Eliminating Majority-Black District Following Supreme Court Ruling
stories.summary:
Louisiana lawmakers approved a new congressional map Friday that eliminates one of the state's two majority-Black U.S. House districts while positioning Republicans to potentially pick up a seat. The state Senate passed the measure 28-10, and Republican Gov. Jeff Landry is expected to sign it into law.

The move follows an April 30 Supreme Court ruling that struck down Louisiana's existing court-ordered map — drawn in 2024 to comply with the Voting Rights Act — as an illegal racial gerrymander. That ruling weakened the landmark 1965 Voting Rights Act and intensified a national redistricting battle, with Louisiana among several Southern states now redrawing maps to benefit Republicans ahead of midterm elections. President Trump has made protecting the GOP's slim House majority a priority.

Republican bill sponsor state Sen. Jay Morris insisted the new map was drawn along partisan, not racial, lines, saying he directed demographers to exclude racial data and told lawmakers he was intentionally concentrating Democrats — not Black voters specifically — into a single district. Democratic state Sen. Sam Jenkins countered that the map amounts to racial gerrymandering that will face further legal challenges: 'I think it's a racially gerrymandered district that's going to get us into a lot of trouble here,' he said. Morris replied, 'Agree to disagree.'

Republicans currently hold four of Louisiana's six congressional seats. The approved 5-1 map was chosen over a more aggressive 6-0 option, which Republicans deemed riskier because it would have required adding more Black voters to GOP-held districts. Legal challenges to the new map are considered likely.

stories.headline: Russia Warns of Escalating Strikes on Kyiv as Putin Seeks to Revive Domestic War Narrative
stories.summary:
Russia has warned of 'consistent and systematic' missile strikes on Kyiv and called for foreign embassies to evacuate the Ukrainian capital, signaling President Vladimir Putin's intention to sharply escalate aerial attacks. Analysts say Putin is seeking to reverse sagging domestic approval ratings and counter growing Russian war fatigue as the conflict enters its fifth year with battlefield advances stalled.

Russia's front-line gains, which had accelerated in 2025, have largely ground to a halt in recent months. The Washington-based Institute for the Study of War assessed that 'the character of the war is shifting in favor of Ukrainian forces, at least for now,' noting that Ukrainian forces have reclaimed some ground and are employing new tactics to break out of positional warfare. Three people were injured Friday in a Russian strike on the city of Zaporizhzhia, with residential buildings damaged.

Moscow has paired its escalatory rhetoric with large-scale nuclear force drills and warnings to European allies against what the Kremlin characterizes as their involvement in Ukrainian drone attacks. Putin's stated objective of quickly capturing the eastern Donetsk region remains unfulfilled, and the battlefield stalemate is undermining his domestic political messaging.

The warnings come amid the broader context of the ongoing U.S.-Iran war, which has diverted Western and U.S. attention and resources. European allies have been ramping up support to Ukraine in that environment, and the prospect of intensified strikes on Kyiv raises the stakes for civilian casualties and international response.

stories.headline: Hegseth Reassures Asian Allies on U.S. Commitment at Shangri-La Dialogue, Calls for Higher Defense Spending
stories.summary:
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth addressed the Shangri-La Dialogue security summit in Singapore on Saturday, seeking to reassure Asia-Pacific allies that the United States was not abandoning the region despite its military commitments in the Iran war. Hegseth rejected suggestions that global obligations meant 'turning our backs' on Asia, saying the U.S. can 'do two things at one time' and was working 'quietly but very strongly' with regional partners.

Japan's Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi pressed Hegseth directly, warning that some countries might 'underestimate' U.S. commitment and seek to 'drive a wedge' between Washington and its allies. Hegseth also faced questions about the U.S. suspension of a $14 billion arms package to Taiwan — done to conserve munitions for the Iran conflict — and insisted the U.S. remained in a 'very strong position' on its overall munitions stockpile. He said he would 'very much decouple' the Taiwan arms issue from broader alliance commitments.

Hegseth used the forum to reiterate demands that Asian allies spend at least 3.5 percent of GDP on defense, praising Japan, South Korea, Australia, and the Philippines for recent increases in military spending and cooperation. His address came hours after Vietnam's President To Lam, delivering the summit's keynote, called for adherence to international law and more dialogue to manage U.S.-China competition, warning that flashpoints like the Strait of Hormuz show how regional crises can rapidly disrupt global trade and energy.

The summit comes weeks after President Trump's positive meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing, adding complexity to U.S. messaging on deterrence versus engagement. Hegseth's emphasis on 'hard power' over 'rules-based order' rhetoric drew implicit contrast with the multilateral tone favored by several other summit participants.
